headline: Fossils are time capsules—ancient life preserved in stone for us to discover
universal_truth: The past leaves traces; everything that exists changes what comes after
fun_facts: Most fossils are of hard parts like bones and shells—soft tissue rarely preserves
The oldest fossils are about 3.5 billion years old—simple single-celled organisms
Less than 0.1% of all species that ever lived left fossils—we know only a tiny fraction of Earth's history
discussion_questions: What 'fossils' will your life leave behind?
How does knowing about extinct creatures change how you see current life?
What stories from the past are you carrying forward?

hook.script: A child finds a rock with a fern printed inside—perfectly preserved from 300 million years ago. That fern died before dinosaurs existed, before mammals, before most of what we know. Yet here it is, a message across time. Fossils are letters from the ancient past.

cliff.script: Most living things just decay when they die. Yet some become fossils that last hundreds of millions of years. What rare circumstances turn something that would normally rot into permanent stone?

options.text: Rapid burial protects remains, then minerals slowly replace organic material
options.response: Yes. Quick burial prevents decay, and over millennia, minerals seep in and turn remains to stone.

options.text: Extreme cold or heat preserves organisms permanently
options.response: Those can preserve briefly, but true fossils involve mineralization...

fact1.title: Mineral Replacement
fact1.script: Fossilization usually requires quick burial in sediment—keeping scavengers and bacteria away. Over thousands to millions of years, minerals dissolved in groundwater seep into bones and shells, gradually replacing organic material molecule by molecule. The shape persists; the substance transforms.

fact2.title: The Rarity of Fossils
fact2.script: Less than 0.1% of all species that ever lived became fossils. Most soft-bodied creatures left no trace. Most environments don't favor preservation. What we know of ancient life comes from a tiny, biased sample. We're reading a book with most pages missing.

fact3.title: Ancient Storytellers
fact3.script: The oldest fossils are 3.5 billion years old—simple bacteria and algae. They tell us life began early and stayed simple for a long time. Then complexity exploded. Fossils narrate Earth's story: slow beginnings, sudden innovations, mass extinctions, and always, persistence.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Everything leaves traces. The way you live, the things you create, the relationships you build—they're fossils in formation. What story will the traces of your life tell those who come after?

outro.script: That's Day 50—fifty days of learning together! Tomorrow, we enter the time of dinosaurs. Until then, consider: what will you leave behind that might last?

growTrack.title: Legacy Thinking - What Will You Leave
growTrack.learning_objective: Consider the traces your life will leave behind
growTrack.activity: Imagine someone discovering 'fossils' of your life in 100 years. What would you want preserved? What traces are you currently creating—in writing, in relationships, in deeds? Create or strengthen one thing today that might last.
